hypotheses.statement: The rise in line markdowns since 2023 is a refrigerant-transition clearance of R-410A (and early R-454B) equipment, not discounting spread across products, channels or the people keying orders. If it is true, markdown dollars outside equipment stay near zero, markdown rates are flat across channels and order-takers, and the R-410A share of markdowns climbs as R-410A volume falls.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: markdown dollars (approximated as shipped value x md/(1-md)) were $4,136,801 in 2022 and $12,000,384 in 2025 (q103), an increase of $7,863,583 (q122). In 2025, 8,295 of 8,318 R-410A equipment lines carried a markdown (q109), and R-410A equipment gross margin fell from 0.1626 in 2022 to 0.0192 in 2025 (q114). Parts, refrigeration and supplies had no markdown lines in 2022 or 2025 (q109). In 2025 the share of lines with a markdown was 0.0719-0.0835 for EDI, web and the top email order-takers (q106). Interpretation: if this is a planned clearance, the money is the price of a regulatory change; if markdowns also run on R-454B and non-refrigerant equipment ($3,828,444 and $3,774,409 in 2025, q109), part of it is avoidable.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: About $7.9M a year more markdown in 2025 than in 2022 (q122, sized from the data). The avoidable part is unknown.
hypotheses.support: Markdown dollars on R-410A rise as R-410A stock ages. Markdowns on R-454B and non-refrigerant equipment are tied to particular SKUs (aged or discontinued) and not to customers or reps. Markdown rates are flat across channel, taken_by and account manager.
hypotheses.weaken: Markdowns on R-454B and non-refrigerant equipment grow as fast as on R-410A. Markdown rates differ sharply by account manager or customer after controlling for SKU. Markdowns start before the transition and do not follow R-410A stock levels.
hypotheses.data_available: Yes. The caveat is that unit_cost is a static snapshot (orient q41), so margin levels over time reflect price only.

hypotheses.statement: Gross margin erosion is broad customer-discount creep across all categories, not only the equipment markdowns in H1. If it is true, price-to-list falls for parts, supplies and refrigeration as well as equipment, and the average customer discount_pct on lines rises year after year because of new or repriced accounts.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: line gross margin fell from 0.2729 (2016) to 0.2258 (2025), and price-to-list fell from 0.8434 to 0.8022 (q101). The average customer discount weighted by lines rose from 0.1415 to 0.1518 (q103). At 2016 gross margin, 2025 revenue of $138,932,581 would have earned about $6.54M more gross margin (q104). Caveat: cost is static (orient q41/q45), so this measures price erosion against today's cost, not real margin.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Up to about $6.5M a year in gross margin (q104, sized from the data). It overlaps with H1 and has to be split from it.
hypotheses.support: Price-to-list falls in categories that never have line markdowns (parts, supplies, refrigeration). The discount creep comes from customers onboarded later at higher discount_pct, or from mix shifting toward high-discount accounts.
hypotheses.weaken: Price-to-list is flat outside equipment, so the whole decline is H1 plus product mix. A mix decomposition (fixed 2016 weights by SKU and customer) leaves little rate effect.
hypotheses.data_available: Partly. discount_pct is a current snapshot with no history, so repricing of existing accounts cannot be seen directly, only inferred from price-to-list per customer over time. There is no cost history.

hypotheses.statement: Hartwell holds R-410A equipment stock that will sell well below historical margin or not at all. If it is true, R-410A equipment on hand at cut-off is large relative to the recent R-410A sales rate, and the 2025 margin collapse continues on the remaining stock.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: R-410A equipment on hand at cut-off is $7,925,628 at master cost across 189 SKUs (q113). R-410A equipment revenue fell to $11,234,489 in 2025 at 0.0192 gross margin (q114). The 2025 margin gap against 2022 margin on that revenue is about $1.61M (q122). Carrying cost at an assumed 20% a year would be about $1.59M (q121; the rate is an assumption).
hypotheses.dollars_rough: About $1.6M a year of margin gap plus about $1.6M a year of carrying cost at an assumed 20%. Exposure on the remaining stock is up to $7.9M (q113, q121, q122).
hypotheses.support: Months of supply for R-410A equipment at the 2025 sales rate exceed 12. Stock is concentrated in branches with falling R-410A sales. Stock POs for R-410A kept arriving after sales began to fall.
hypotheses.weaken: R-410A stock at cut-off covers only a few months of 2025 sales. Stock POs for R-410A stopped early. Remaining units are selling steadily.
hypotheses.data_available: Yes for stock and sales. Future sell-through and write-off policy are not in the records.

hypotheses.statement: Vendor bills with an invoice number ending in '-R' are duplicates of an already-billed PO, and Hartwell pays a material share of them. If it is true, each paid '-R' bill matches an earlier bill on the same PO for the same amount, both bills are paid, and no vendor credit offsets the second payment.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: 1,429 '-R' bills total $4,196,810.04. 963 of them were paid, $2,732,286.38 in all (q98), about $273k a year over 10 years (q98).
hypotheses.dollars_rough: About $273k a year (q98, sized from the data).
hypotheses.support: The original bill on the same PO was paid as well. No matching finance_vendor_credits row exists. The rate is concentrated in particular vendors.
hypotheses.weaken: The originals turn out to be unpaid (the '-R' replaces them rather than adding to them). Paid '-R' bills sit on POs with a second receipt. Vendor credits net them out.

hypotheses.statement: Vendors bill above the PO (higher unit cost, higher quantity, or added freight) and Hartwell's three-way match lets most of it through. If it is true, bills over PO value are mostly paid in full rather than short-paid to the PO, and the excess is concentrated in particular vendors.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: excluding '-R' bills, 20,121 bills have line value above PO value, $4,584,727.82 in excess. 13,901 of them were paid in full, carrying $3,149,433.24 of excess (q99), about $315k a year (q121). Separately, freight on bills totals $3,007,927.95, of which $2,081,728.12 sat on bills paid in full, about $208k a year (q120). Interpretation: some of this may be legitimate price increases that were never updated on POs. Without contract prices it cannot be called overbilling, only payment above PO.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: About $315k a year of above-PO line value plus about $208k a year of freight paid (q120, q121, sized from the data).
hypotheses.support: The excess is concentrated by vendor. Receipt quantities (always equal to PO, orient q92) contradict billed quantities above PO. Short-pay versus full-pay of similar bills does not depend on any visible attribute.
hypotheses.weaken: Above-PO unit costs are uniform across a vendor's SKUs from a given date (a price increase). Paid-in-full bills cluster on vendors whose freight terms are known to be collect.
hypotheses.data_available: Mostly. Vendor contract prices and freight terms are missing, so 'right' versus 'wrong' cannot be settled. The q99 count (20,121) excludes '-R' bills, so it differs from the orient figure of 20,194.

hypotheses.statement: Goods shipped and never invoiced are a steady billing leak, not a cut-off timing effect. If it is true, uninvoiced shipped lines occur at a stable rate every year, they are never invoiced later, and they cluster in a fulfilment type, branch or order pattern (for example multi-ship orders).
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: 5,932 lines with shipped quantity above invoiced quantity, $3,773,119.33 at line price. 434-627 lines a year from 2016 to 2024, and 1,437 lines in 2025 (q100), part of which is likely cut-off. The 2016-2024 average is about $285k a year (q121).
hypotheses.dollars_rough: About $285k a year of revenue, 2016-2024 average (q121, sized from the data).
hypotheses.support: The rate is stable outside the last weeks before cut-off. The lines concentrate in transfer or partial-ship orders, or in orders with several invoices. WMS sale movements confirm the goods left stock.
hypotheses.weaken: The WMS shows no sale movement for these lines (goods never left, so qty_shipped is wrong rather than billing). Or they are concentrated in the fractional-quantity opening-balance artefact of 2016.

hypotheses.statement: Short lines (stock unavailable at order) are lost sales that also push customers away. If it is true, customers who had short lines order less, or stop ordering, in the following months compared with similar customers who did not.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: short lines are 0.0325-0.1203 of lines a year (q105), and their ordered value at line price is $6,976,265-$24,088,619 a year (q105). Gross margin on those lines averages about $2.66M a year (q122). Interpretation: if customers re-order the same SKU within days, little is lost.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Up to about $2.7M a year of gross margin (q122, sized from the data). The true loss depends on the re-order rate.
hypotheses.support: Few short lines are followed by an order for the same customer and SKU within about 10 operating days. Customers with high short rates have lower next-year retention and revenue growth than matched customers.
hypotheses.weaken: Most short lines are re-ordered shortly afterwards by the same customer. Short rates have no relation to later customer activity once branch, size and season are controlled for.
data: wms_inventory_transactions (stock on hand at order day)
hypotheses.data_available: Weakly. There is no backorder or cancel record (orient q9), so re-orders can only be inferred from later orders, and this hypothesis is the hardest to test cleanly.

hypotheses.statement: Customer attrition is concentrated in particular branches or account managers (outside rep_id) rather than spread evenly. If it is true, the share of active customers with no orders the next year differs materially between branches or reps after controlling for customer size and trade.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: each year 272-465 active customers placed no order the next year (q110). Their prior-year revenue averaged about $8.44M a year from 2016 to 2024 (q121). At 2025 to 2016 gross margin (0.2258-0.2729, q101) that is about $1.90M-$2.30M a year of margin (q123). Interpretation: some lapse is normal (contractors closing or retiring).
hypotheses.dollars_rough: About $8.4M a year of revenue from lapsing customers, $1.9M-$2.3M of margin (q121, q123, sized from the data). Only the excess above a base rate is avoidable.
hypotheses.support: Lapse rates vary by branch or rep well beyond chance (binomial intervals). Lapse follows observable friction such as short lines, returns, invoice-question contacts or late special orders.
hypotheses.weaken: Lapse rates fall within noise across branches and reps. Lapsed customers are small and new (onboarding churn), not established accounts.
hypotheses.data_available: Partly. There are no churn dates, and rep assignment is a current snapshot, so a customer's rep at the time of lapse is unknown.

hypotheses.statement: Differences in quote win rate between outside reps are explained by their customers' standing discount levels, not by the reps, and extra quote markdowns do not buy wins. If it is true, win rate tracks the customer's discount_pct, and quotes with line markdowns win no more often than quotes without.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: rep win rates range from 0.3563 to 0.5336, overall 0.429 (q118). Quotes lost on 'price' total $185,039,838 over 10 years (q118), about $18.5M a year (q121). Win rate is 0.4295 for quotes with no markdown and 0.4209-0.4266 with markdowns (q119), so markdowns show no lift. The rep with the lowest win rate (72) also has the lowest average customer discount (0.09, q102). Interpretation: the markdowns may then be margin given away for nothing.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: $18.5M a year of quote value lost on price (q121). The recoverable share is not yet sized and is likely a small fraction (interpretation).
hypotheses.support: Within customers of similar discount_pct, rep win rates converge. Within the same customer, quotes with markdowns win at the same rate as quotes without.
hypotheses.weaken: Rep spread survives controls for customer discount, branch and quote size. Markdown quotes win clearly more often within the same customer and SKU mix.
hypotheses.data_available: Mostly. There are no competitor prices, and 29,340 lost quotes have no reason (orient q67).

hypotheses.statement: A material share of inventory is excess against demand. If it is true, a large value sits in SKU-branch positions holding more than two years of supply at the 2025 sales rate, and those positions keep receiving stock POs.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: on hand at cut-off is $32,929,866 at master cost. $10,450,263 sits in SKU-branches with more than two years of 2025 sales on hand, and $2,603,550 in 507 SKU-branches with no 2025 sales (q108). Carrying cost at an assumed 20% a year on the over-two-years stock is about $2.09M (q121; the rate is an assumption). Overlaps with H3 for R-410A.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: About $2.1M a year of carrying cost at an assumed 20% (q121, the rate is assumed).
hypotheses.support: Excess positions persist for years and keep getting stock POs. Transfers between branches seldom draw them down.
hypotheses.weaken: The excess is mostly seasonal equipment that turns in the next season, or slow-moving parts that are cheap to hold. Removing R-410A leaves little.
hypotheses.data_available: Yes, at static cost. There are no cycle counts or shrink records (orient q30), so book stock is assumed to be real.

hypotheses.statement: Late customer payment ties up working capital, and the lateness is concentrated in a small set of customers or terms rather than spread evenly. If it is true, a minority of customers accounts for most of the dollar-days past due.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: across 1,366,817 paid invoices, late payments average 8.34 operating days past due. The dollar-weighted average late balance is about $2,902,415 (q107). At an assumed 8% cost of capital that is about $232k a year (q107). Caveat: payments look generated (always one payment for the full amount, orient q18).
hypotheses.dollars_rough: About $232k a year at an assumed 8% cost of capital (q107).
hypotheses.support: The top decile of customers by late dollar-days holds most of the total. Lateness differs by terms_days or credit limit use.
hypotheses.weaken: Lateness is uniform across customers (consistent with a generated payment schedule). Late dollar-days are small relative to the credit limits.
hypotheses.data_available: Yes, though the payment records may not reflect real behaviour.

hypotheses.statement: OEM special orders arriving later than the vendor's quoted lead time cause repeat 'Special order ETA' and 'Order status' contacts. If it is true, ETA contacts per special order rise with days late, and contact volume follows the late share over time.
hypotheses.why_it_matters: Observed: 26,362 of 120,693 OEM special lines (0.2184) shipped more than 5 operating days after the vendor's quoted lead (q115, q121). Service contacts run to about 1,908 logged hours a year (q121), with 3,755-9,880 'Special order ETA' contacts a year (q112). Interpretation: the direct staff cost is the smallest of the twelve. The larger cost is probably goodwill, which ties back to H8.
hypotheses.dollars_rough: Small direct cost: about 1,908 hours a year of logged contact time across all subjects (q121). Dollars depend on a loaded labour rate that is not in the records.
hypotheses.support: Customers with late special orders log more ETA contacts in the following weeks (matched through the PO number in notes). Yearly ETA contacts track the late share.
hypotheses.weaken: ETA contacts per special order are flat regardless of lateness. The contact volume is driven by the 2016 spike or by seasonal order volume rather than by delays.
hypotheses.data_available: Partly. The contact-to-order link is only the PO number in notes, about half of contacts (orient q80). Minutes are tightly banded and may not be real handling time. Special POs have no receipt.

notes: Dollar figures use static master unit_cost (no cost history), so all margin numbers are price-against-today's-cost.
Carrying-cost rates (20% for inventory, 8% for receivables) are assumptions, not data.
Rankings: significance reflects likely avoidable dollars a year; answerability reflects whether the records hold the keys and history needed for a clean test. The two orders differ on purpose.
